Let  
\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i),\qquad \bar T_n=\frac1n S_n,
\]
and write \(\eta_\theta=\eta(\theta)\). I take tests below to be level \(\alpha\), \(0<\alpha<1\). Also, uniqueness of the MLE is meant “whenever the MLE exists” and under the usual full natural-parameter-space convention, i.e. the canonical parameter space is an interval.

---

## (a) Sufficient statistic and MLE

The joint density is

\[
L(\theta;x_1,\dots,x_n)
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\exp\left\{\eta(\theta)\sum_{i=1}^n T(x_i)-nB(\theta)\right\}.
\]

Thus

\[
L(\theta;x_1,\dots,x_n)
=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\right)
\exp\{\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta)\}.
\]

By the Neyman–Fisher factorization theorem,

\[
\boxed{S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)}
\]

is sufficient for \(\theta\).

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\theta)
= C(x)+\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta).
\]

Equivalently, in the canonical parameter \(\eta\),

\[
\ell(\eta)
= C(x)+\eta S_n-nA(\eta)
= C(x)+n\{\eta \bar T_n-A(\eta)\}.
\]

Hence the canonical MLE satisfies

\[
\widehat\eta
\in \arg\max_{\eta}\{\eta \bar T_n-A(\eta)\}.
\]

If the maximizer is interior, then the score equation is

\[
0=\frac{d}{d\eta}\ell(\eta)
= n\{\bar T_n-A'(\eta)\},
\]

so

\[
A'(\widehat\eta)=\bar T_n.
\]

Thus, when \(A'\) is invertible and the solution lies in the parameter space,

\[
\boxed{\widehat\eta=(A')^{-1}(\bar T_n)}
\]

and therefore

\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta=\eta^{-1}(\widehat\eta)}
\]

when \(\eta\) is one-to-one. More generally, the MLE set is

\[
\{\theta:\eta(\theta)=\widehat\eta\}.
\]

If \(\bar T_n\) lies outside the range of \(A'\), then the likelihood is maximized, if at all, at the boundary of the natural parameter space.

---

## (b) Relation between \(A(\eta)\) and \(B(\theta)\)

The canonical normalizing function is

\[
A(\eta)
=
\log \int h(x)\exp\{\eta T(x)\}\,dx.
\]

Since the original density is normalized,

\[
1=\int h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)-B(\theta)\}\,dx,
\]

so

\[
B(\theta)
=
\log\int h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)\}\,dx.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{B(\theta)=A(\eta(\theta)).}
\]

If \(\eta\) is one-to-one, then for \(\eta=\eta(\theta)\),

\[
\boxed{A(\eta)=B(\eta^{-1}(\eta)).}
\]

More clearly, writing \(u\) for the canonical parameter,

\[
\boxed{A(u)=B(\theta(u)),\qquad \theta(u)=\eta^{-1}(u).}
\]

---

## (c) Uniqueness of the MLE

Assume \(T(x)\) is not constant on the support and \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one.

The natural parameter space is convex. For \(\eta_1\neq \eta_2\) and \(t\in(0,1)\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
A(t\eta_1+(1-t)\eta_2)
&=
\log\int h(x)\exp\{(t\eta_1+(1-t)\eta_2)T(x)\}\,dx\\
&=
\log\int \bigl(h(x)e^{\eta_1T(x)}\bigr)^t
          \bigl(h(x)e^{\eta_2T(x)}\bigr)^{1-t}\,dx.
\end{aligned}
\]

By Hölder’s inequality,

\[
\int \bigl(h e^{\eta_1T}\bigr)^t
          \bigl(h e^{\eta_2T}\bigr)^{1-t}
\le
\left(\int h e^{\eta_1T}\right)^t
\left(\int h e^{\eta_2T}\right)^{1-t}.
\]

Taking logs gives

\[
A(t\eta_1+(1-t)\eta_2)
\le
tA(\eta_1)+(1-t)A(\eta_2).
\]

Equality in Hölder would imply

\[
h(x)e^{\eta_1T(x)}
=
c\,h(x)e^{\eta_2T(x)}
\]

for some constant \(c>0\), hence

\[
e^{(\eta_1-\eta_2)T(x)}=c
\]

on the support. Since \(\eta_1\neq \eta_2\), this would force \(T(x)\) to be constant on the support, contrary to assumption. Therefore the inequality is strict:

\[
A(t\eta_1+(1-t)\eta_2)
<
tA(\eta_1)+(1-t)A(\eta_2).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{A(\eta)\text{ is strictly convex}.}
\]

Equivalently, under the usual regularity conditions,

\[
A'(\eta)=\mathbb E_\eta[T(X)],
\qquad
A''(\eta)=\operatorname{Var}_\eta(T(X))>0,
\]

because \(T(X)\) is not almost surely constant.

Now the canonical log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\eta)=C+n\{\eta\bar T_n-A(\eta)\}.
\]

Since \(-A(\eta)\) is strictly concave, \(\ell(\eta)\) is strictly concave. A strictly concave function on an interval has at most one maximizer. Hence the canonical MLE \(\widehat\eta\), if it exists, is unique.

Because \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one, there is at most one \(\theta\) corresponding to \(\widehat\eta\). Therefore

\[
\boxed{\text{the MLE of }\theta\text{ is unique whenever it exists}.}
\]

---

## (d) Most powerful test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta=\theta_1\), \(\theta_1>\theta_0\)

Let

\[
\eta_0=\eta(\theta_0),\qquad \eta_1=\eta(\theta_1).
\]

Since \(\eta(\theta)\) is strictly increasing and \(\theta_1>\theta_0\),

\[
\eta_1>\eta_0.
\]

The likelihood ratio is

\[
\frac{L(\theta_1)}{L(\theta_0)}
=
\exp\left\{
(\eta_1-\eta_0)S_n
-n[B(\theta_1)-B(\theta_0)]
\right\}.
\]

Because \(\eta_1-\eta_0>0\), this likelihood ratio is a strictly increasing function of \(S_n\).

By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects for large values of the likelihood ratio, equivalently for large values of \(S_n\). Since \(S_n\) is continuous, no randomization is needed. Choose \(c_\alpha\) so that

\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

Then the MP level-\(\alpha\) test is

\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha(X_1,\dots,X_n)
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}.
}
\]

---

## (e) UMP test for \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\)

For \(\theta'>\theta\),

\[
\frac{L(\theta')}{L(\theta)}
=
\exp\left\{
(\eta(\theta')-\eta(\theta))S_n
-n[B(\theta')-B(\theta)]
\right\}.
\]

Since \(\eta(\theta')>\eta(\theta)\), this likelihood ratio is increasing in \(S_n\). Therefore the family has a monotone likelihood ratio in the statistic \(S_n\).

By the Karlin–Rubin theorem, the upper-tail test is UMP for one-sided alternatives.

Explicitly, choose \(c_\alpha\) satisfying

\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

Define

\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha(X_1,\dots,X_n)
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}.
}
\]

Because the family is stochastically increasing in \(\theta\),

\[
\theta\le \theta_0
\implies
\mathbb P_\theta(S_n>c_\alpha)
\le
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)
=
\alpha.
\]

Therefore the test has level \(\alpha\) for the composite null.

Now fix any \(\theta_1>\theta_0\). By part (d), the same test is most powerful of level \(\alpha\) for testing

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_1.
\]

Any test of level \(\alpha\) for the composite null also has size at most \(\alpha\) at \(\theta_0\), so by the Neyman–Pearson lemma it cannot have larger power at \(\theta_1\). Since \(\theta_1>\theta_0\) was arbitrary, \(\varphi_\alpha\) is UMP.

Thus the UMP level-\(\alpha\) test is

\[
\boxed{
\text{Reject }H_0\text{ iff } \sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)>c_\alpha,
\qquad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
}
\]

---

## (f) Existence of a UMP test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta\neq\theta_0\)

Assume \(\theta_0\) is an interior point of the parameter space, so that there exist both \(\theta_+>\theta_0\) and \(\theta_-<\theta_0\). For \(0<\alpha<1\), there is generally no UMP level-\(\alpha\) test for the two-sided alternative.

Suppose, for contradiction, that a UMP level-\(\alpha\) test \(\varphi\) exists.

First take \(\theta_+>\theta_0\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the unique MP level-\(\alpha\) test for

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_+
\]

rejects for large \(S_n\). Thus there exists \(c_U\) such that

\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_U)=\alpha,
\]

and the unique MP test is

\[
\varphi_U=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_U\}.
\]

If \(\varphi\) is UMP against all \(\theta\neq\theta_0\), it must in particular be MP against \(\theta_+\). Hence

\[
\varphi=\varphi_U
\quad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Now take \(\theta_-<\theta_0\). Since \(\eta(\theta_-)-\eta(\theta_0)<0\), the likelihood ratio is decreasing in \(S_n\). Therefore the unique MP level-\(\alpha\) test for

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_-
\]

rejects for small \(S_n\). Thus there exists \(c_L\) such that

\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n<c_L)=\alpha,
\]

and the unique MP test is

\[
\varphi_L=\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_L\}.
\]

Again, if \(\varphi\) were UMP, it would have to satisfy

\[
\varphi=\varphi_L
\quad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Therefore we would need

\[
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_U\}
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_L\}
\quad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

But this is impossible for \(0<\alpha<1\). Indeed, both rejection regions have probability \(\alpha\) under \(\theta_0\), but one is an upper tail and the other is a lower tail. Since \(S_n\) is continuous, the two sets cannot coincide almost surely.

Therefore no such UMP test exists.

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\text{For a genuine two-sided alternative and }0<\alpha<1,
\text{ there is no UMP level-}\alpha\text{ test.}
}
\]

Only trivial exceptions occur: if \(\alpha=0\) or \(\alpha=1\), or if \(\theta_0\) is a boundary point so that the alternative is effectively one-sided.

H_1:\theta=\theta_1.
\]

Any test of level \(\alpha\) for the composite null also has size at most \(\alpha\) at \(\theta_0\), so by the Neyman–Pearson lemma it cannot have larger power at \(\theta_1\). Since \(\theta_1>\theta_0\) was arbitrary, \(\varphi_\alpha\) is UMP.

Thus the UMP level-\(\alpha\) test is

\[
\boxed{
\text{Reject }H_0\text{ iff } \sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)>c_\alpha,
\qquad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
}
\]

---

## (f) Existence of a UMP test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta\neq\theta_0\)

Assume \(\theta_0\) is an interior point of the parameter space, so that there exist both \(\theta_+>\theta_0\) and \(\theta_-<\theta_0\). For \(0<\alpha<1\), there is generally no UMP level-\(\alpha\) test for the two-sided alternative.

Suppose, for contradiction, that a UMP level-\(\alpha\) test \(\varphi\) exists.

First take \(\theta_+>\theta_0\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the unique MP level-\(\alpha\) test for

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_+
\]

rejects for large \(S_n\). Thus there exists \(c_U\) such that

\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_U)=\alpha,
\]

and the unique MP test is

\[
\varphi_U=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_U\}.
\]

If \(\varphi\) is UMP against all \(\theta\neq\theta_0\), it must in particular be MP against \(\theta_+\). Hence

\[
\varphi=\varphi_U
\quad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Now take \(\theta_-<\theta_0\). Since \(\eta(\theta_-)-\eta(\theta_0)<0\), the likelihood ratio is decreasing in \(S_n\). Therefore the unique MP level-\(\alpha\) test for

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_-
\]

rejects for small \(S_n\). Thus there exists \(c_L\) such that

\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n<c_L)=\alpha,
\]

and the unique MP test is

\[
\varphi_L=\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_L\}.
\]

Again, if \(\varphi\) were UMP, it would have to satisfy

\[
\varphi=\varphi_L
\quad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Therefore we would need

\[
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_U\}
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_L\}
\quad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

But this is impossible for \(0<\alpha<1\). Indeed, both rejection regions have probability \(\alpha\) under \(\theta_0\), but one is an upper tail and the other is a lower tail. Since \(S_n\) is continuous, the two sets cannot coincide almost surely.

Therefore no such UMP test exists.

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\text{For a genuine two-sided alternative and }0<\alpha<1,
\text{ there is no UMP level-}\alpha\text{ test.}
}
\]

Only trivial exceptions occur: if \(\alpha=0\) or \(\alpha=1\), or if \(\theta_0\) is a boundary point so that the alternative is effectively one-sided.
